desc:
A chess knight may start on any cell of an empty m x n board. One move changes the position by (±1, ±2) or (±2, ±1) and must stay on the board. The knight may visit cells repeatedly.

Count the walks of exactly k moves, where a walk is the list of visited cells (including the starting cell), and return the count modulo 1,000,000,007. A walk of 0 moves is just a starting cell.

m = 3, n = 4, k = 1  ->  28
m = 3, n = 3, k = 2  ->  32   (the centre cell has no moves)
m = 4, n = 4, k = 3  ->  464
m = 2, n = 4, k = 5  ->  8     (every cell has exactly one move)
hints: Layer-by-layer DP over the moves costs O(k · cells), which is far too slow for k up to a billion. Look at the structure of one layer step.
One DP step is the same linear map every time: new = A · old, where A is the adjacency matrix of the knight graph (at most 16 × 16).
Raise A to the k-th power by repeated squaring, apply it to the all-ones vector (one walk of length 0 from every cell), and add up the entries. Keep every product modulo 1,000,000,007.
editorial: Number the cells 0..s-1 (s = m · n ≤ 16) and let A[i][j] = 1 when a knight can jump from cell i to cell j. If v[t][i] is the number of walks of t moves that start anywhere and end at cell i, then v[t+1] = AT v[t]; since A is symmetric the transpose does not matter. Starting from v[0] = (1, ..., 1), the answer is the sum of the entries of Ak v[0].

Compute the power with binary exponentiation: keep P = A<sup>2<sup>i</sup></sup> by repeated squaring, and whenever bit i of k is set replace the vector v by P v. Powers of the same matrix commute, so the order does not matter, and only squarings cost s<sup>3</sup>. In total that is about 30 matrix squarings of size at most 16, i.e. roughly 30 · 4096 multiplications, plus 30 cheap matrix-vector products. Everything is taken modulo 1,000,000,007 so that numbers stay small.
Edge cases: k = 0 gives exactly m · n walks, and boards on which the knight can never move (such as 1 × n or 2 × 2) give 0 for every k ≥ 1.
